key_insight: A finite-temperature quantum quasinormal-mode theory describes lossy, non-reciprocal cavity magnonic systems while accounting for material dissipation, radiation leakage, and thermal fluctuations.
engineering_relevance: The framework supports quantitative design of hybrid photon–magnon–qubit devices under realistic open-system and thermal conditions.
method: Combine macroscopic quantum electrodynamics for non-reciprocal media with complex coordinate transformations.
Quantize quasinormal modes in spatially inhomogeneous, dissipative, and dispersive magnonic resonators.
Apply the theory to hybrid dielectric–magnonic resonators coupled to spin and superconducting qubits.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical applications showing modal interference, a coherent-to-dissipative coupling transition, spatiotemporal quantum field dynamics, and magnon-mediated qubit synchronization at zero and finite temperatures.
watch_item: The abstract provides no experimental validation or quantitative accuracy benchmarks, leaving device-level predictive performance to be established.
paper_title: Finite-temperature Quantum Quasinormal Mode Theory for Spatiotemporally-resolved Dissipative Cavity Quantum Magnonics
